title: New license request: MIT License with Proof-of-Usage Condition (MIT-PoU), v1.2.0
body:
**Third filing, and the settled one.** [#3064](https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/issues/3064) was closed when its tag was superseded; [#3065](https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/issues/3065) tracked the licence through `v1.1.1` and `v1.2.0` by edits, and its history reads like the drafting it was. This request replaces it, filed clean at **`v1.2.0`** — the version whose wording is settled — with the adoption list current. The prior issue is closed with a pointer here.

### How license meets inclusion principles

Taking the principles in order — the definitive factors first, then the others — including where
this licence does not meet them.

#### Definitive factors

**A. It does not match a licence already on the list.** Checked against the SPDX matching
guidelines and `DOCS/license-match.md`. The permission grant is MIT verbatim, but the licence adds
a substantive condition — roughly forty lines defining a record obligation, a credits obligation
and the hash that ties them together — which no listed licence contains. Its nearest relative in
effect rather than wording is BSD-4-Clause, whose advertising clause is a different obligation in
different words. If the Legal Team reads the matching guidelines as reaching this, I would rather
be told than have a duplicate listed.

**B. Not OSI-approved,** so this factor does not apply. Stated again under factor 1 below.

**C. It is a source licence.** The grant is MIT: source is distributed under it, and the added
condition does not restrict source availability in any way.

**D. The text is identifiable and stable, and is not in the midst of drafting.** Frozen at tag
`v1.2.0`, and that is the text pasted below. The version history, stated rather than left to a
diff: `v1.1.1` changed the heading of `v1.0.1` to carry the short identifier; `v1.2.0` reworded
the record clause to state what the markup notes always intended — the provenance branch name is
a suggestion, any branch that accepts pull requests serves, and absent a designation the default
branch is the designated one. The grant, both halves of the condition and the hash rule are
unchanged since `v1.0`.

**E. The steward commits to stability.** I am the steward, and the text at `v1.2.0` will not be
modified after addition to the list: the tag stays where it points, and no revision of those terms
is published under it or under the identifier `MIT-PoU`. A change to the terms would be a new
version at a new tag, submitted as a separate request with its own identifier, so that anything
already labelled `MIT-PoU` keeps meaning exactly what it means today. Documentation around the
licence may continue to change; the licence file at the tag will not.

#### Other factors

**1. Compliance with an open source definition — it does not, and I am not claiming otherwise.**
The added condition places an obligation on a class of user, which the OSD does not permit. This
falls to be considered under factor 4 instead: the licence is intended for free distribution of
source with limited restrictions. The grant is MIT in full — use, modify, sell, sublicense, no
payment, no revenue share, no field-of-use limit. What it adds is a disclosure obligation on
operators of automated systems: record the use in the repository, and name the work in the credits
of whatever that use produced. If the Legal Team's reading is that factor 1 is definitive and
factor 4 does not reach this, that is a fair outcome and I would rather hear it than have it
listed on a misunderstanding.

**2. Generally usable by anyone.** Yes. It is published as a template with `[Year]` and
`[Copyright Holders]` placeholders, plus tooling (`npx proof-of-usage licence`) and a validation
workflow. It names no project, company or consortium. The provenance branch name and record
filename are given as suggestions in the text itself as of `v1.2.0`. The underlying
record/credit/hash mechanism is additionally specified licence-independently, as the public-domain
[Proof of Usage PoU/1.0](https://github.com/origami-ltd/proof-of-usage), usable beside unmodified
MIT, Apache-2.0 or GPL as a request — this licence is the variant where the request is a
condition, and it is submitted on its own terms rather than as the only way to the mechanism.

**3. Actual, substantial use.** Seven repositories, and I will not dress the number up. Four are
mine — the wasm.ltd game-preservation projects and the licence's own repository. Three are not,
all adopted within four days of publication:

- [mrxenginner/reVC](https://github.com/mrxenginner/reVC) (~257 stars) — the reverse-engineered
  GTA Vice City codebase, whose maintainers had previously declined to attach any licence at all.
  Adopted 13 August 2026 in [reVC#37](https://github.com/mrxenginner/reVC/pull/37).
- [Polyphase-Labs/Polyphase-Engine](https://github.com/Polyphase-Labs/Polyphase-Engine) (~55
  stars) — a game engine, previously unlicensed. Adopted 16 August 2026 in
  [Polyphase-Engine#50](https://github.com/Polyphase-Labs/Polyphase-Engine/pull/50), merged by the
  project's own maintainer account, with its own copyright holder in the notice
  (`Copyright (c) 2022 Martin Holtkamp`) and the register and discovery document both present.
- [gumiranda/cloudfunding](https://github.com/gumiranda/cloudfunding) — adopted 14 August 2026,
  with the caveat that its copyright notice names its author and me jointly.

Disclosed rather than left to be found: I proposed all three as pull requests; the maintainers
reviewed and merged them. That is how a new licence reaches anyone, but a reviewer should hear it
from me. If the answer is still "come back when there is more", that is reasonable and I will.

**4. Free distribution with limited restrictions.** Yes — see 1.

**5. Steward's position.** I am the steward and I am making this request.

**Markup notes for the XML.** `[Year]` and `[Copyright Holders]` are the standard replaceable
copyright fields. As of `v1.2.0` the branch-name flexibility is stated in the clause itself rather
than needing markup. Some adopting repositories append a project-specific appendix *after* the
licence text, naming a service that opens the required pull request for systems that cannot open
one themselves; that is an offer by those projects and not part of these terms, and appended text
should sit outside the identifier for matching purposes.

**1.** License name: Archive Packaging Exception
**2.** Short identifier: Archive-packaging-exception
**3.** License author or steward: ale5000
**4.** Comments: This exception addresses a specific gap in the current SPDX License List regarding the distribution of software in aggregated, compressed, or containerized formats.
While existing exceptions focus on software linking (API/Library), this proposal focuses on the Packaging Process.

Possible uses:

1) System and Platform Modding: In ecosystems such as mobile platforms, custom firmware, and embedded systems, GPLv3-licensed automation scripts must be bundled into installable archives (e.g., flashable ZIPs).
These archives often require the inclusion of independent third-party modules or assets with incompatible licenses. This exception provides a clear legal framework to treat these as "Independent Modules" within the same distribution container.

2) Containerization (Docker and OCI Images): As software moves toward containerized distribution, users often build images where GPLv3 components coexist with proprietary or differently licensed tools.
This exception clarifies that such bundling—where components interact through standard interfaces—does not extend the copyleft requirements to the entire container image.

3) Modern CI/CD and Security Compliance: Modern distribution requires archives to be validated and digitally signed.
This exception explicitly protects the use of digital signing tools, code coverage, and profiling analysis tools within an "Eligible Packaging Process," ensuring that security and quality compliance do not conflict with the license terms.

4) Protection of Copyleft Integrity: A key feature of this exception is the explicit exclusion of derivative works.
It ensures that "Independent Modules" must be truly independent under copyright law. If a module is based on the GPLv3 components, it remains subject to the full GPLv3 requirements, thus preventing any "weakening" of the core copyleft protections.
